The foundational structure of cognitive-motor skill theory synthesis begins with phenomenological description, capturing the experiential essence of skill execution. This is followed by multilevel mechanistic analysis—incorporating biomechanics, motor control, expertise, and cognition—to build a comprehensive model. The third step involves systematizing findings into sport-specific theories. A key operational framework emerges from Huesmann and Loffing’s 7-level classification of perception-action coupling, which defines stimulus presentation and response mode orientation. This classification enables rigorous experimental design and analysis of anticipation in racquet sports. Dual-task performance modeling reveals that acute cognitive-motor interference leads to performance deterioration, whereas chronic training enhances dual-task capabilities. These primitives form a coherent epistemic chain: from subjective experience to objective measurement, from static models to dynamic systems, and from isolated tasks to integrated skill execution.
